questions.stem: A roster service builds the weekend schedule with `Schedule weekend = new Schedule(List.copyOf(weekday.shifts()));`, where `weekday.shifts()` returns the weekday schedule's own `ArrayList` and `Shift` is a class with a `setNurse(String)` method. A planner then calls `weekend.shifts().get(0).setNurse("Jane Doe")`. What happens to the weekday schedule's first shift?

options.text: Its nurse is now Jane Doe, since the weekend list holds the same Shift objects as the weekday list
options.says: List.copyOf makes a new list of the same references, so a change to an element through one list is a change to the element of the other

options.text: Its nurse is now Jane Doe, since both schedules hold one and the same list object
options.says: List.copyOf returns a new list; what the two lists share is their elements

options.text: It keeps its nurse, since List.copyOf put a copy of each Shift into the new list
options.says: List.copyOf copies the references, not the objects they refer to

options.text: It keeps its nurse, since the call throws UnsupportedOperationException on the unmodifiable list
options.says: an unmodifiable list refuses add and remove; it can't stop a call on one of its elements

origin.section: A Copy Is Only as Deep as the Code That Made It

questions.stem: A service reads `mode` from a properties file at startup and later runs `if (mode == "strict") enableStrictChecks();`. Its unit test constructs the service with `new Service("strict")`, and the test passes. In production the file says `mode=strict`. What does the service do in production?

options.text: It enables the strict checks, since == compares the characters of the value read from the file with the literal's
options.says: == on references is true only for one object; it never looks at the characters

options.text: It enables the strict checks, since the JVM gives the value read from the file the same object as the literal
options.says: only literals and compile-time constants share one object; a String read at run time is a new object

options.text: It skips the strict checks, since the value read from the file is a different String object from the literal
options.says: the test passed because both sides were the same literal object; the value parsed at run time is another object with the same characters

options.text: It skips the strict checks, since the literal in the check is a new String object each time that line runs
options.says: the JVM keeps one object per literal, so every run of that line uses the same object; that is why the test passed

origin.section: == Compares References; equals Compares What the Class Defines

questions.stem: A booking screen runs `Seat[] row = new Seat[12];` and then `for (Seat s : row) if (s.isFree()) free++;`. `Seat` is a class with a public no-argument constructor that marks the seat free. What happens?

options.text: The loop counts 12 free seats, since creating the array runs Seat's no-argument constructor for each element
options.says: creating an array of references creates no objects; each element starts as null

options.text: The loop counts 0 free seats, since isFree() called on an element that holds no object returns false
options.says: calling a method on a null reference throws NullPointerException; it returns nothing

options.text: The first pass of the loop throws NullPointerException, since every element of the new array is null
options.says: array elements of a reference type start as null, and s.isFree() on null throws

options.text: The compiler rejects the loop, since it reads the array's elements before anything assigns them
options.says: only local variables must be assigned before they are read; array elements get a default value

origin.section: A Reference Field or Array Element Starts as null, and the NPE Comes Where It Is Used

questions.stem: On logout a service removes the user's `Session` from a static `Map<String, Session>`. The `Session` and its `Basket` still refer to each other, and nothing else refers to either. The JVM runs with default settings, and no code calls `System.gc()`. What happens to the two objects?

options.text: A later collection can free both of them, since nothing that a root leads to refers to either one
options.says: the collector keeps only what it can reach from the roots; references inside an unreachable cycle don't count

options.text: A later collection can free the Session but not the Basket, since the map entry that was removed held the Session
options.says: the Basket is referred to only by the Session, so once the Session is unreachable the Basket is too

options.text: Neither is freed while they refer to each other, since each one still holds a strong reference to the other
options.says: the JVM doesn't count references; an unreachable cycle is garbage

options.text: Neither is freed before code calls System.gc(), since the JVM starts a collection when the program asks for one
options.says: the JVM collects on its own as the heap fills; System.gc() is only a request to collect now

origin.section: An Object Lives While Something Reachable Refers to It
